paragraphs: “Oh, blast it!... I jumped down to get a look at the man I’d hurt ... I couldn’t tell you why!”
“Though you were worked up and running away?”
“Yes, worked up and running away, and I still jumped down.”
“You wanted to help him?”
“Help!... Yes, maybe I did want to help him.... I can’t remember.”
“You can’t remember? So you weren’t altogether aware of what you were doing?”
“Not at all. I remember everything—every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and I wiped his face with my handkerchief.”
“We’ve seen your handkerchief. Were you hoping to bring him round?”
“I don’t know if I hoped that. I only wanted to find out whether he was alive or dead.”
“Ah! You wanted to find out? Well, and what then?”
“I’m no doctor. I couldn’t tell. I ran off thinking I’d killed him. And now he’s recovered.”
“Excellent,” the prosecutor remarked. “Thank you. That’s all I wanted to hear. Please go on.”

Alas! It never crossed Mitya’s mind to tell them, though he remembered it well, that he had gone back out of pity, and that standing over the man lying there he had even spoken a few words of regret: “You’ve come to grief, old man—there’s no help for it. Well, there you must lie.”

The prosecutor could draw only one conclusion: the man had gone back “at such a moment, and in such agitation, simply to find out whether the _only_ witness of his crime was dead; and so he must be a man of great strength, coolness, resolve and foresight, even at such a moment,” ... and so on. The prosecutor was well pleased. “I’ve provoked this nervous fellow with ‘trifles,’ and he’s said more than he meant to.”
Mitya went on, struggling painfully. But this time Nikolay Parfenovitch cut in right away.
“How was it that you ran to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands so smeared with blood, and, it seems, your face as well?”
“Why, at the time I never noticed the blood at all,” Mitya answered.
“That’s quite likely. It happens sometimes.” The prosecutor exchanged a look with Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“I just didn’t notice. You’re quite right about that, prosecutor,” Mitya agreed all at once.

Next came the story of how Mitya had suddenly resolved to “step aside” and leave the way clear for their happiness. But he could not bring himself to open his heart to them the way he had before and tell them about “the queen of his soul.” He hated talking about her in front of these cold men “who were fastening on him like bugs.” So, in answer to their repeated questions, he spoke briefly and curtly:

“Well, I decided to kill myself. What did I have left to live for? That question stared me in the face. Her first, rightful lover had come back, the man who’d wronged her but had hurried back after five years to offer her his love and make amends by marrying her.... So I knew it was all over for me.... Behind me was disgrace, and that blood—Grigory’s.... What was there to live for? So I went to redeem the pistols I’d pawned, to load them and put a bullet through my head tomorrow.”
“And a grand feast the night before?”

“Yes, a grand feast the night before. Oh, damn it all, gentlemen! Do hurry up and get this over with. I meant to shoot myself not far from here, out beyond the village, and I’d planned to do it at five in the morning. I even had a note in my pocket by then. I wrote it at Perhotin’s while I was loading the pistols. Here’s the letter. Read it! I’m not saying this for your sake,” he added with contempt. He pulled it from his waistcoat pocket and threw it onto the table. The lawyers read it with interest and, as usual, filed it with the papers of the case.
“And it didn’t even occur to you to wash your hands at Perhotin’s? You weren’t afraid of drawing suspicion?”

“What suspicion? Suspicion or none, I’d have galloped straight here just the same and shot myself at five o’clock, and you’d have been too late to do anything. If it weren’t for what happened to my father, you’d have known nothing and wouldn’t have come here at all. Oh, it’s the devil’s doing. The devil murdered father, and it’s thanks to the devil that you found out so fast. How did you get here so quickly? It’s marvelous, it’s a dream!”

“Mr. Perhotin told us that when you came to him, you were holding ... in your bloodstained hands ... your money ... a lot of money ... a bundle of hundred-rouble notes, and that his servant-boy saw it too.”
“That’s true, gentlemen. I remember that’s how it was.”

“Now, there’s one small point that arises. Can you tell us,” Nikolay Parfenovitch began, very gently, “where you got so much money all of a sudden, when the facts and the timing show that you had not been home?”
The prosecutor’s brows drew together at the question being put so bluntly, but he did not interrupt Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“No, I didn’t go home,” Mitya replied, looking perfectly calm but keeping his eyes on the floor.

“Then let me ask again,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, as if creeping up on the subject. “Where could you possibly have found such a sum all at once, when, as you admit yourself, at five o’clock that same day you—”

“I needed ten roubles, so I pawned my pistols with Perhotin, and then I went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she wouldn’t give me, and so on, and all the rest of it,” Mitya cut in sharply. “Yes, gentlemen, I needed money, and then suddenly there were thousands, eh? Do you know, gentlemen, what you’re both afraid of right now? ‘What if he won’t tell us where he got it?’ Well, that’s just how it is. I’m not going to tell you, gentlemen. You’ve guessed right. You’ll never know,” said Mitya, chipping out each word with extraordinary determination. The lawyers were silent for a moment.
“You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it’s vitally important for us to know,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, in a soft, smooth voice.
“I understand. But I still won’t tell you.”

The prosecutor stepped in too. He reminded the prisoner once more that he was free to decline to answer questions if he judged that to be in his interest, and so on. But given the harm he might do himself by his silence, especially in a case as grave as—

“And so on, gentlemen, and so on. Enough! I’ve heard that rigmarole before,” Mitya broke in again. “I can see for myself how important it is, and that this is the crucial point, and I still won’t say.”
“What does it matter to us? It’s not our affair, it’s yours. You’re hurting yourself,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch nervously.

“Look, gentlemen, joking aside”—Mitya raised his eyes and looked at them both steadily—“I had a feeling from the very beginning that we’d clash at this point. But at first, when I started giving my evidence, it was all still far off and hazy; it was all floating about, and I was so naive that I began by assuming we trusted each other. Now I can see for myself that there can be no such trust, because sooner or later we were bound to run into this cursed stumbling-block. And now we’ve run into it! It’s impossible, and that’s the end of it! But I don’t blame you. You can’t believe it all just because I say so. I understand that, of course.”
He sank back into gloomy silence.

“Could you not, while keeping your resolve to say nothing about the main point, at least give us some small hint of what kind of motives are strong enough to make you refuse to answer, at a moment so dangerous for you?”
Mitya gave a sad, almost dreamy smile.

“I’m a lot more good-natured than you think, gentlemen. I’ll tell you why, and I’ll give you that hint, though you don’t deserve it. I won’t speak of it, gentlemen, because it would stain my honor. The answer to the question of where I got the money would bring me far greater disgrace than murdering and robbing my father would, if I had murdered and robbed him. That’s why I can’t tell you. I can’t, for fear of the disgrace. What, gentlemen, are you going to write that down?”
“Yes, we’ll write it down,” lisped Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You shouldn’t write that down, about ‘disgrace.’ I only told you out of the goodness of my heart. I didn’t have to tell you. I made you a present of it, so to speak, and you pounce on it right away. Oh, well, write—write whatever you like,” he finished, in scornful disgust. “I’m not afraid of you, and I can still look you in the eye.”
“And can you not tell us what sort of disgrace it is?” Nikolay Parfenovitch ventured.
The prosecutor scowled darkly.
“No, no, _c’est fini_, don’t bother. It isn’t worth dirtying one’s hands. I’ve dirtied myself enough on your account already. You’re not worth it—nobody is ... Enough, gentlemen. I’m not going on.”
He said this too firmly to be argued with. Nikolay Parfenovitch did not press him further, but from Ippolit Kirillovitch’s eyes he could see that the prosecutor had not given up hope.
“Could you at least tell us how much money you had in your hands when you walked into Mr. Perhotin’s—how many roubles, exactly?”
“That I can’t tell you.”
“You told Mr. Perhotin, I believe, that you had three thousand from Madame Hohlakov.”
“Maybe I did. Enough, gentlemen. I won’t say how much I had.”
“Then would you be good enough to tell us how you came here, and what you’ve done since you arrived?”
“Oh! You can ask the people here about that. But I’ll tell you, if you like.”

He proceeded to tell it, but we won’t repeat his story. He told it dryly and curtly. About the raptures of his love he said nothing; he only said that he had dropped his plan of shooting himself because of “new factors in the case.” He gave the story without going into reasons or details. And this time the lawyers did not badger him much. It was plain that nothing here was of any essential interest to them.

“We’ll check all that. We’ll return to it when we examine the witnesses, which will, naturally, be done in your presence,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch in conclusion. “And now let me ask you to put on the table everything you have on you, above all any money you still have.”

“My money, gentlemen? Certainly. I understand that’s needed. I’m actually surprised you didn’t ask about it sooner. It’s true I couldn’t have got away anywhere. I’m sitting here in plain sight. But here’s my money—count it—take it. That’s everything, I think.”

He turned out all his pockets; even the small change—two twenty-copeck pieces—he dug out of his waistcoat pocket. They counted the money. It came to eight hundred and thirty-six roubles and forty copecks.
“And is that all?” the investigating lawyer asked.
“Yes.”
“A moment ago you stated in your evidence that you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikovs’. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, you lost two hundred here, then....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch went through all of it. Mitya helped him willingly. They recalled every last farthing and put it in the sum. Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly added up the total.
“With these eight hundred, you must have started with about fifteen hundred?”
“I suppose so,” Mitya snapped.
“Why does everyone claim there was much more?”
“Let them claim it.”
“But you claimed it yourself.”
“Yes, I did, too.”

“We’ll compare all this with the evidence of other people we haven’t yet questioned. Don’t worry about your money. It will be properly looked after and will be returned to you at the end of ... what is now beginning ... if it appears, or, so to speak, is proved, that you have an undisputed right to it. Well, and now....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly stood up and told Mitya firmly that it was his duty and obligation to carry out a minute and thorough search “of your clothes and everything else....”
“By all means, gentlemen. I’ll turn out every pocket, if you like.”
And he really did begin to turn out his pockets.
“You’ll need to take off your clothes as well.”
“What! Undress? Ugh! Damn it! Won’t you search me as I am? Can’t you?”
“It’s quite out of the question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You must take your clothes off.”
“Have it your way,” Mitya gave in gloomily; “only please, not here, but behind the curtains. Who’s going to search them?”
“Behind the curtains, naturally.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch nodded his assent. His small face had a look of peculiar solemnity.
